items.title: Predicting Glass Transition Temperature of Polyimide Homopolymers and Copolymers Using Interpretable QSPR-Based Machine Learning: The MFKit Framework
items.abstract_or_text: In this work, we address the problem of predicting the glass transition temperature of polyimides, a class of high-performance engineering thermoplastics, with an emphasis on both homopolymer and copolymer systems. While machine learning approaches have been widely applied to polymer property prediction, their extension to copolymers remains limited and often lacks the interpretability required for rational materials design. To overcome these limitations, we develop an interpretable QSPR-based framework (MFKit) that combines physically grounded descriptors for monomer featurization with Gaussian Process Regression (GPR). The model is trained on a dataset of polyimide homopolymers from PoLyInfo and achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art approaches (R2 = 0.856, MAE = 20.7 °C on the test set). Causal inference and SHAP analysis reveal key structure–property relationships, identifying aromatic content, backbone flexibility and rotation, side chain volume and hydrogen bonding as dominant factors governing Tg. The framework is subsequently extended to polyimide copolymers by constructing copolymer representations through combination of monomer descriptor vectors using several aggregation schemes. The best-performing approach yields R2 = 0.832 and MAE = 23.3 °C on an external dataset compiled from the literature. Furthermore, guided by the identified structure–property relationships, polyimide copolymers are designed, synthesized, and experimentally characterized, each exhibiting increased Tg compared with the parent homopolymer. Validation against DSC measurements demonstrates strong agreement with predictions (MAE = 16.3 °C). Overall, the proposed approach provides a unified and interpretable framework for Tg prediction for both homopolymer and copolymer systems, enabling physically grounded and data-driven design of polyimide-based materials.

items.title: ReproBAIT: Can coding agents build their own biological AI tools?
items.abstract_or_text: Large language models are increasingly competent at leveraging scientific knowledge and existing computational tools to execute complex workflows. At present, little information exists on their ability to reconstruct tools when given limited descriptions of such tools. We introduce an evaluation titled ReproBAIT (Reproducing Biological AI Tools), which measures the ability of coding agents to design, implement, and train biological AI tools taken from published research across a range of information access conditions. The coding agent is securely sandboxed without internet access and receives training data, a fixed time and compute budget, and limited information about the tool to replicate. We then score the reproduced biological AI tool based on its performance (tool-specific metrics) on held-out data. We evaluated a set of biological AI tools of varying complexities: ProteinMPNN, an inverse protein folding tool, RFdiffusion3, an all-atom generative diffusion tool, and a closed-source molecular design tool. We institute a methodology to check for memorisation, as the open source tools are likely to be included in models' pretraining corpus. Across a range of leading closed- and open-source coding agents, we find substantial reproduction capability for some selected tools, though limited capability for a highly complex tool. We find moderate evidence consistent with memorisation, varying across coding agents. These results suggest that tool developers need to be increasingly cautious when releasing information about the tools publicly; re-creation of the tool based on such information could undermine a tool's commercial value or invalidate dual-use managed access strategies.

items.title: Gas-Conditioned Message Passing Graph Neural Network for Permeability Prediction in Polymeric Membranes
items.abstract_or_text: Designing polymeric membranes for diverse gas-separation applications remains a critical challenge. Machine learning (ML) models can significantly accelerate this effort by capturing complex relationships between polymer-gas pairs and enabling permeability prediction over an extended chemical space of gases and polymers. In this work, we present a novel ML framework, the gas-conditioned message passing neural network (GC-MPNN), that jointly combines gas descriptors and polymer chemistry in a fused neural network model. Polymers are represented at the monomer level and encoded as molecular graphs, where node and edge information is propagated through message-passing layers. Six gas species (He, H2, N2, O2, CH4, and CO2) are represented using multiple descriptor sets spanning thermodynamic, kinetic, and electrostatic properties, along with one-hot encodings and combined feature sets that include kinetic plus thermodynamic descriptors and the full physicochemical descriptor set. For each descriptor combination, model hyperparameters are optimized using Bayesian optimization within a leave-one-gas-out (LOGO) validation framework. Test performance is then evaluated on the gas species excluded entirely from the corresponding training fold (out-of-training set) and compared across descriptor sets. For most gas species, the model achieves strong predictive performance (R2 ∼ 0.86–0.96), while CO2 remains more challenging in terms of absolute prediction accuracy (R2 ∼ 0.44). Active learning sampling further improves model performance by adding a few labeled samples from the test gas species into the training set. Among the three strategies tested, deep ensemble-based sampling and random sampling show strong improvement, with R2 reaching approximately ∼ 0.95 for all gas species, while evidential regression shows less consistent improvement. The model is further evaluated on a smaller polymer-gas dataset containing hydrocarbon species (C2H4, C2H6, C3H6, C3H8, and n-C4H10) using the GC-MPNN trained only on the six base gases, achieving moderate to strong Pearson correlations (r ∼ 0.77–0.89) for these out-of-training gases. Overall, this work presents a machine learning model that can learn transferable polymer-gas relationships from known gas species and extend them to previously unseen gases.

items.title: PhySGA: A Physics-Space Grounded Agentic Framework for Generalizable and Interactive 3D Composition
items.abstract_or_text: 3D object composition is pivotal to digital content creation and robot simulation, while also serving as a critical testbed for physical intelligence in foundation models. Previous methods either leverage large language models to directly predict object coordinates, or utilize generative diffusion priors to synthesize composite images for visual alignment, both of which rely on static priors in digital spaces. However, these methods consistently struggle with complex compositions such as precise hanging, gravity-driven settling and hidden containment, as these tasks require interactive construction processes involving global planning, fine-grained alignment, and physical simulation. To address these challenges, we propose PhySGA, a Physics-Space Grounded Agentic Framework for 3D composition via agent exploration and physical simulation, enabling the universal interactive assembly of rigid, articulated, and deformable objects. Directly applying vanilla LLMs or VLMs to this task proves insufficient, as current models inherently lack grounded physical understanding and interactive construction experience. To overcome this limitation, we design a collaborative feedforward-feedback architecture: an Assembly Agent focuses on geometric and kinematic reasoning for global step planning and coarse adjustment, while a Critic Agent reasons over contact dynamics for simulator state diagnosis and fine-grained closed-loop correction. Furthermore, Action Routers map semantic planning and analysis onto executable physical primitives within the simulator, while a task-specific Self-Evolving Skill Library distills historical trial-and-error feedback into reusable experiences, boosting success rates and minimizing exploration attempts. Extensive experiments within Isaac Sim demonstrate that PhySGA significantly surpasses existing methods in relation fidelity, physical plausibility, and visual quality.

items.title: OmniScore: Universal Scoring of Diverse Biomolecular Complexes via Equivariant Geometry-Aware Discrete Representation Learning
items.abstract_or_text: Biomolecular structures provide a common physical basis for understanding molecular function and interactions. However, computational models typically specialize in individual molecular classes or tasks, hindering a unified representation of structural information across biological systems. Here we introduce OmniScore, a universal geometric encoder that learns shared representations of proteins, nucleic acids, small molecules and their complexes. Pretraining integrates geometric graph encoding, sequential modeling and tokenization with structural and physicochemical supervision. The frozen pretrained encoder supports complex-level model quality assessment and interaction prediction, as well as residue-level prediction, through task-specific heads. OmniScore outperforms the evaluated antibody--antigen quality-assessment baselines and also improves RNA structure ranking over baselines. For peptide-major histocompatibility complex interaction prediction, the OmniScore embeddings complement structure-prediction confidence metrics to improve predictive performance. Together, these findings support OmniScore as a shared geometric foundation for biomolecular representation and scoring across molecular classes and prediction scales, which may facilitate multi-component therapeutics development.

items.title: PolyNet: A Python Package for Polymer Informatics
items.abstract_or_text: Polymers are used in a wide range of industries for diverse applications but formulating them to attain desired properties remains a challenging task. Polymer informatics has emerged as a powerful approach for the rational design of materials. Here, we present PolyNet, an open-source Python package that provides an end-to-end workflow for polymer informatics. PolyNet: 1) reads and validates datasets of polymer properties, including the monomer structures and their molar ratios; 2) creates vector- and graph-based representations of the polymers; 3) trains and optimises traditional machine learning (ML) models and graph neural networks (GNNs); 4) compares representations and models statistically; 5) deploys the models to screen in silico libraries of polymers, flagging polymers outside the applicability domain of the models and estimating their expected prediction error; and 6) interprets the models to understand structure–property relationships. PolyNet provides unique features such as: modelling of homopolymers and copolymers with any number of components, using the molar ratio of monomers in both vector- and graph-based representations; acceptance of textual representations of monomers or repeating units; calculation of polyBERT fingerprints and PolyMetriX and RDKit descriptors and fingerprints and accepting standalone user precalculated representations; benchmarking of all representation–model combinations on identical data splits using paired statistical tests; and chemically interpretable explanations through fragment-level attribution for GNNs and SHAP analysis for traditional ML models. Every experiment automatically records its configuration, data splits, hyperparameter search spaces and trained models, supporting full reproducibility in line with FAIR principles. PolyNet can be used through Python scripts, a command-line interface, or a graphical user interface for researchers without programming experience. We exemplify PolyNet by two case studies: glass transition temperature prediction for homopolymers, where cluster-based data splits showed that random splits overestimate model performance, the applicability domain identified less reliable predictions, and the model explanations recovered the known effect of chain mobility on T g ; and ¹⁹F MRI signal-to-noise ratio prediction for copolymers, where encoding monomer molar ratios is key to accurate predictions.

items.title: Text-Informed Training Data Filtering for Enhanced Virtual Flow Meter Performance
items.abstract_or_text: In sectors such as energy, aquaculture and chemical processing, the effectiveness of both mechanistic and data-driven models is frequently limited by poor-quality training data, which obscures underlying physical laws and degrades predictive accuracy. Such quality issues commonly manifest as anomalies in the dataset, ranging from sensor faults to process upsets and incorrect operator inputs. While traditional rule-based filtering can remove a subset of the anomalies, it is unable to leverage contextual information stored as unstructured text, such as engineer comments and operational logs that explain under what conditions the data was collected. We propose a text-informed data filtering method that leverages large language models (LLMs) to integrate unstructured operational data with tabular sensor data. The method consists of two steps: (1) contextual anomaly detection by reasoning over both data modalities, and (2) generation of a binary mask that is applied to filter the training dataset for model development. To investigate the potential benefit, a steady-state soft-sensor regression model, namely a virtual flow meter that estimates well flow rates, is used as the downstream evaluation target. Experiments on a synthetic oil and gas dataset show improved model performance compared to traditional rule-based filtering. Ablation studies show that textual operator comments can provide filtering-relevant signals beyond sensor data alone, with the multimodal approach reducing downstream MAPE from 7.1% to 5.4% relative to sensor-only filtering. This work demonstrates that integrating unstructured operational knowledge with sensor data through LLMs can improve data quality for industrial machine learning applications, offering a scalable alternative to manual data curation.

items.title: ProtModernBERT: Compute-Efficient Protein Language Modeling
items.abstract_or_text: Large protein language models provide a powerful framework for learning sequence-function relationships and guiding experimental design. However, architectural improvements are underexplored, especially in low-compute regimes of relevance for resource-constrained research laboratories. We show that the training cost for encoder-only transformer architectures can be reduced by leveraging modern architectural refinements, offering an encouraging performance / compute-efficiency trade-off. We introduce ProtModernBERT, a modernized BERT-style model pre-trained on amino acid sequences, and compare it with ProtBert, Amplify, and ESM2 across a set of supervised structural tasks -encompassing secondary structure prediction, disorder prediction, and subcellular localization- and ProteinGym's zero-shot functional benchmark. We find that ProtModernBERT matches or closely tracks the performance of Amplify-120M and ProtBert with up to 80-90\% reduction in pre-training FLOPs, and narrows the gap to ESM2 when controlling for pre-training. Our analysis using a cluster-based validation protocol for hyperparameter selection and randomly initialized models disentangles the contributions of architecture and data, showing that modern components provide stronger inductive biases that are more consequential than parameter count in low-compute regimes.

items.title: Machine Learning Prediction of Subsequent Drug Release Trajectories using Early Release Information in PLGA Microparticles
items.abstract_or_text: Accurate prediction of drug-release behavior from PLGA microparticles may reduce the experimental effort required for formulation characterization, yet conventional prediction approaches rely primarily on static molecular and formulation descriptors and do not incorporate experimentally observed release behavior as it becomes available during an ongoing experiment. Here, we develop a machine-learning framework that integrates molecular and formulation descriptors with early-release measurements to predict subsequent drug-release trajectories from PLGA microparticles. A dataset comprising 4,913 release observations from 321 formulations was analyzed using random forest regression with formulation-grouped cross-validation. Using a common set of 89 formulations, we systematically evaluated the predictive value of increasing amounts of early-release information. Prediction accuracy improved with additional early measurements, but the incremental benefit progressively diminished, with two and three measurements capturing 64.7% and 91.9% of the total predictive gain achieved with four measurements, respectively. The value of early information also varied substantially across formulations, with greater benefits generally observed for formulations that were more difficult to predict from static descriptors alone. Trajectory-level analysis further revealed that early observations constrained subsequent release trajectories to different extents across formulations. These findings demonstrate that experimentally observed early-release behavior provides formulation-specific predictive information beyond static descriptors and establish a data-driven framework for quantifying information sufficiency in drug-release characterization.

items.title: Into the Unknown: Benchmarking AI agents on open scientific research problems
items.abstract_or_text: Can AI agents carry out research on open scientific problems? We introduce Into the Unknown, a benchmark that provides an agent with a science paper along with a research direction to pursue and tasks it to write a follow-up paper. We work with scientists at US Department of Energy (DOE) national laboratories, who each contribute an unpublished follow-up direction from their own work together with the necessary conditions a submission must meet. While assessing the quality of a follow-up paper is challenging in general, using these conditions to form a rubric makes evaluation more tractable for research problems that have no reference answer. We have nine frontier agents write 15 follow-ups each, spanning quantum computing, plasma physics, computational chemistry, materials science, and scientific machine learning domains. None of the 135 submissions satisfies all the conditions, and 114 fail our integrity check, most often because the paper claims work that was never done or reports numbers that contradict the recorded evidence. Overall, agents readily produce papers that look like follow-ups, but none meets the standard of the domain scientist, leaving substantial headroom. Our code and data are publicly available.

items.title: MFG: Multi-turn Feedback Guided Molecular Optimization
items.abstract_or_text: Multi-objective molecular optimization is a critical process in drug discovery that aims to modify a given molecule to simultaneously improve multiple properties while maintaining a similar overall structure. This process often requires iterative modifications guided by computational or experimental feedback. Recent large language model (LLM)-based methods have begun to explore this iterative approach; however, these methods are not explicitly trained to leverage such feedback, while existing approaches primarily focus on single-turn molecular optimization. To address this gap, we introduce Multi-turn Feedback Guided (MFG) molecular optimization, a reinforcement learning framework that trains an LLM to progressively optimize molecules using feedback from previous turns. MFG introduces a feedback vector capturing both property improvements and source molecule similarity, alongside a feedback-aligned reward function that promotes progressive improvement across turns. We apply MFG over GeLLM^{3}O, a state-of-the-art LLM model for multi-objective molecular optimization, evaluate GeLLM^{3}O-MFG on ten multi-objective molecular optimization tasks. The results demonstrate that GeLLM^{3}O-MFG achieves the highest average similarity-constrained success rate (81.50%), outperforming the base model GeLLM^{3}O (70.81%).

items.title: H-DDCM: Hadamard Codebooks for Fast Generative Image and Video Compression
items.abstract_or_text: Training-free diffusion-based compression methods repurpose the generative priors of a diffusion or a flow model to compress data without retraining them as task-specific codecs. Recent codebook-based approaches such as Turbo-DDCM achieve strong perceptual quality at ultra-low bitrates, but their reliance on dense Gaussian codebooks remains costly in both memory and computation, and scales poorly with the large latent dimensions of modern image and video generators. Their combinatorial bitstream encoding further becomes computationally heavy at this scale. We introduce H-DDCM, a scalable generative compression framework that replaces Gaussian codebooks with implicit randomized Hadamard dictionaries. The fast Walsh-Hadamard transform allows for implicitly synthesizing full-dimensional dictionaries with O(d \log d) compute for projection and reconstruction and O(d) memory, without materializing the full-dimensional dictionary. We further introduce an efficient table-free lexicographic coding scheme that makes combinatorial encoding practical at larger dimensions. Beyond images, we adapt the framework to an autoregressive video flow model and develop a streaming compression scheme that periodically re-encodes recently reconstructed frames into a fresh KV-cache prefix, preserving temporal context across segments at no additional transmitted bits. This enables long-form, close to real-time generative video compression on a single GPU. Across image and video benchmarks, H-DDCM achieves competitive rate-distortion-perception performance while substantially reducing the memory and computational overhead of codebook-based training-free generative compression.

items.title: QUPEX: A Streamlit-Based Framework for Visualizing Quantum-Mechanical Property Spaces of Organic Molecules
items.abstract_or_text: The growing availability of quantum-mechanical (QM) datasets offers new opportunities to investigate structure-property and property-property relationships in drug-like molecules using data-driven methods. However, interactive tools that integrate molecular visualization, statistical analysis of QM properties, clustering, and machine learning (ML) remain limited, despite their value in facilitating dataset exploration and interpretation. To address this gap, we introduce QUPEX (QUantum Property EXplorer), an open-source Streamlit-based framework for the interactive exploration of QM property spaces in molecular systems. As a demonstration, we apply QUPEX to a subset of the QM7-X dataset comprising 41,537 equilibrium molecular structures containing up to seven non-hydrogen atoms (C, N, O, S, and Cl) and their 24 associated QM properties. In addition to property-space analysis, QUPEX incorporates an XGBoost regression pipeline for predicting PBE0 dipole moments from tight-binding-derived electronic descriptors, together with model evaluation and SHAP-based interpretability functionality. By combining interactive molecular visualization, data analysis, and predictive modeling, QUPEX provides an accessible and extensible environment for investigating molecular datasets and identifying patterns in their structural and electronic properties. These capabilities can support the exploration of chemical space and inform the rational design of drug-like molecules with targeted QM properties.

items.title: PerSo: Investigating Facets of LLMs' Social Intelligence in Real-World Persuasion Scenarios
items.abstract_or_text: Understanding the social intelligence of large language models (LLMs) is increasingly important for applications involving human-AI interaction and multi-agent environments. Social intelligence comprises two aspects: cognitive intelligence, the ability to infer others' mental states, and behavioral intelligence, the ability to select appropriate social actions based on these inferences to achieve social goals. Persuasion provides a natural testbed in which both aspects are simultaneously at play, yet prior benchmarks typically evaluate them in isolation using synthetic scenarios. We introduce PerSo, a benchmark that evaluates both aspects on real-world persuasion dialogues from Reddit's ChangeMyView community, using an LLM-in-the-loop pipeline to construct the evaluation tasks, validated through human annotation. Our evaluation of diverse LLMs shows that performance generally scales with model size but varies across dimensions. The strongest LLM slightly surpasses the best observed human performance on the behavioral task, while the best human participant remains ahead on the cognitive task.

items.title: SEA-HELM Audio: Evaluating Multilingual ASR-LLM Pipeline Performance Across SEA-HELM Subsets
items.abstract_or_text: We introduce SEA-HELM Audio, a Southeast Asian (SEA) multilingual evaluation framework that extends the text-based SEA-HELM benchmark to assess performance degradation in cascaded automatic speech recognition and large language model (ASR-LLM) pipelines. Using synthesized speech, we compare speech-input and text-input performance across five languages (Chinese, English, Malay, Indonesian, and Tamil) on multiple-choice reasoning and instruction-following tasks. We evaluate open-weight and commercial ASR-LLM systems using identical verifiers and quantify the speech gap as the difference between text and speech accuracy. Results show substantial degradation, with accuracy drops of 9.00 to 18.50 percentage points for multiple-choice reasoning and 20.00 to 42.86 points for instruction following. Tamil exhibits the largest degradation, exceeding 40 percentage points. Our findings highlight the limitations of text-only benchmarks in predicting voice-agent reliability and demonstrate the value of SEA-HELM Audio for evaluating multilingual voice-agent systems.

items.title: Physics-Informed Deep Learning in Oncology
items.abstract_or_text: Deep learning has enabled substantial advances in oncology, including cancer detection and diagnosis, medical image analysis, tumor characterization, treatment planning, response assessment, and outcome prediction. However, conventional data-driven models often require large annotated datasets, exhibit limited generalization across heterogeneous clinical settings, and lack explicit mechanisms for incorporating the physical, physiological, and biological principles underlying cancer development and treatment. Physics-informed deep learning (PIDL) integrates governing physical laws, mechanistic models, physiological constraints, and domain knowledge into deep learning frameworks, providing a principled approach for learning from sparse, noisy, and heterogeneous oncological data. This review presents a task-oriented synthesis of PIDL methods across oncology, encompassing neural networks, Kolmogorov-Arnold networks, convolutional and vision architectures, neural operators, generative models, and hybrid physics-data-driven frameworks. Their applications are examined across cancer detection and diagnosis, image reconstruction and analysis, tumor characterization, quantitative imaging, tumor progression, treatment response, radiation therapy, treatment planning, and multimodal clinical modeling. Based on the synthesized methodological and application-level evidence, we develop task-optimized PIDL workflows that align the clinical task with appropriate data representations, physical constraints, model architectures, and validation strategies. We further analyze key challenges, including physical-model fidelity, computational scalability, uncertainty quantification, domain generalization, standardized benchmarking, and clinical validation.

items.title: Extrapolating Collisional Rate Coefficients for Molecules of Astrophysical Interest Using Neural Networks
items.abstract_or_text: State-to-state rate coefficients for inelastic molecular collisions are essential inputs for non-local thermodynamic equilibrium radiative transfer models, yet their computation using quantum scattering methods is prohibitive for large molecules and highly excited rotational states. We investigate the ability of artificial neural networks to extend existing datasets of collisional excitation rate coefficients without performing additional scattering calculations. A multilayer perceptron model was trained using molecular quantum numbers, level energies, energy gaps, and kinetic temperature as descriptors, and optimized on logarithmic rate coefficients. The model was tested on diverse collision systems ranging from simple diatomic molecules (CO, SiO) to open-shell species (SO), small asymmetric tops (H_2O, SO_2), and complex organic molecules (benzonitrile and vinyl cyanide) colliding with H_2 molecules or He atoms. Extrapolations were performed toward higher rotational levels, higher temperatures, and combinations of both. For most systems, predictions of rate coefficients involving previously unseen rotational states yielded mean error factors between 1.1 and 1.5, with the dominant rate coefficients generally reproduced more accurately than weaker transitions. Temperature extrapolations proved particularly successful, while combined extrapolations in temperature and rotational levels remained accurate to within a factor of two in most cases. The prediction quality depends on the interplay between dataset size, temperature range, molecular complexity, and the presence of clear collisional propensity rules. Overall, the approach demonstrates that machine learning can provide a practical route to extending collisional datasets for astrophysical applications, especially for large molecules for which additional quantum-scattering calculations are computationally demanding.

items.title: Constructed Negatives Shape the Evaluation of Sequence-Based Protein--Protein Interaction Models
items.abstract_or_text: Many machine-learning tasks, including representation learning, rely on negative examples that are constructed rather than directly observed. This issue is especially important for protein--protein interaction (PPI) prediction, where experimentally established non-interactions are scarce. PPI models are therefore commonly trained and evaluated against sampled, unobserved protein pairs treated as negatives. We study how this construction affects model comparison. Keeping positives, protein-disjoint splits, class balance, and model selection fixed, we vary training and evaluation negatives independently across six constructions and four sequence-based models, three of which use protein language model (pLM) representations. Changing only the test negatives shifts AUPRC by up to 0.26, and the top-ranked architecture changes with the construction. Negatives matched to true partners in pLM representation space reduce all pLM-based models to near-chance performance, and shuffling partners within each class shows that the original pairing contributes little to AUROC. Constructed training negatives rarely outperform uniform sampling: on external data, they underperform it in 108 of 120 comparisons for the pLM-based models, with gains never exceeding 0.05 AUROC and losses up to 0.23. We release splits, negative-generation procedures, and evaluation code that allow training and evaluation negatives to be varied separately. Our results show that with constructed negatives, model comparisons are not just noisy but systematically sensitive to how negatives are defined, a methodological choice that is often left implicit.

items.title: DiffuChannel: A Conditional Denoising Diffusion Model that Synthesises Single-Molecule Patch-Clamp Data with Exactly Known Idealisation (Ground Truth)
items.abstract_or_text: Development of computational models for single-channel patch-clamp analysis is hampered by limited availability of labelled (idealised) data. Since experiment alone cannot provide a genuine ground truth, two simulation methods are commonly employed; Stochastic sampling from a specified Markov model, augmented with synthetic noise allows creation of unlimited, flawlessly idealised/annotated datasets, yet its authenticity hinges entirely on the premises underlying data and noise generation. A more recent method uses GAN-based generation, this also replicates real-world noise and artefacts, but does not include a ground truth idealisation or annotation and training is notoriously unstable. Here, we introduce DiffuChannel, a conditional noise-removal diffusion model that addresses these drawbacks. Channel dynamics come directly from a user-defined discrete-time Markov chain (or a model fitted to biological seed data), thus, the state assignment for each synthetic trace is precisely determined by design. The diffusion model is then trained exclusively to capture the noise distribution of raw current conditioned on a given idealisation, thereby replicating genuine noise, filtering, and artefact patterns observed in real data without needing to hand craft noise models. We use a two-step coarse-to-fine workflow that starts with a defined slow-envelope component conditioned on longer-term dwell-time features extracted from the input idealisation. This allows a degree of baseline drift and time-dependent relaxations to be captured over timescales far longer than the network's field of view. At generation time, we use a context-preserving inpainting method that enables creation of relatively seamless traces of any desired duration. We demonstrate that with only a limited set of labelled seed traces, synthetic records yield realistic all-points amplitude distribution, noise power spectrum, autocorrelation pattern, and slow envelope comparable to the source data. The model achieves a maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) between windowed real and generated data of 0.005 (median across the five phenotypes). This compares to a within real-split-half MMD value of 0.002 and an amplitude-matched white noise MMD value of 0.108. In this paper, we benchmark this against DeepGANnel. Since the underlying Markov model is defined rather than estimated, DiffuChannel generates infinite, perfectly labelled, phenotype-consistent training data ideal for developing and testing idealisation algorithms. We find that, in practice, this new method is far more stable than previous GAN models and runs start to end without human intervention. We provide the model open-source along with an interactive web-based training and synthesis interface/app.

items.title: AIRRI: Towards a Human-Readable, Machine-Resistant Reading Interface
items.abstract_or_text: The rapid advancement of image-to-text extraction systems and large language models (LLMs) poses new challenges for educational assessment by making assignment materials easy to transcribe and solve with minimal human effort. To address this problem, we present AIRRI (Artificial Intelligence Resilient Reading Interface), a framework for generating machine-resistant educational content, a dataset of higher-education assignments for evaluation, and an initial evaluation of the human readability of AIRRI machine-resistant text designs. AIRRI employs two categories of machine-resistance techniques. First, AIRRI applies image transformations including character spacing, word spacing, line spacing, character opacity variation, stripe overlays, and image noise. Second, AIRRI applies decision-based adversarial attacks: RayS, SurFree, and ADBA. We evaluate AIRRI against three image-to-text systems: Tesseract, EasyOCR, and the transformer-based GOT-OCR2 model. Our results show that AIRRI substantially degrades automated text extraction performance. AIRRI increased character error rates for EasyOCR (6.9% to 55.9%), Tesseract (2.3% to 100.0%), and GOT-OCR2 (30.7% to 48.1%). Word error rates increased for EasyOCR (24.9% to 96.7%) and Tesseract (10.7% to 100.0%). Among the evaluated decision-based attacks, ADBA consistently produced the largest degradation in image-to-text performance, while RayS and SurFree produced more moderate reductions. EasyOCR and Tesseract were generally more susceptible to both image-based and adversarial perturbations than the transformer-based GOT-OCR2 model. Our findings suggest that AIRRI can significantly reduce the reliability of image-to-text-to-LLM workflows, increasing the effort required for AI-assisted assignment completion.

items.title: Does Pretraining Teach Chemical Language Models Chemistry?
items.abstract_or_text: Chemical language models (CLMs) are pretrained on large corpora of molecules with the aim of learning representations that transfer to diverse downstream tasks. Here, we systematically study the effects of pretraining using a series of such CLMs across 64 molecular property prediction datasets. We find that the downstream gains of pretraining in CLMs do not scale and performance saturates below gradient-boosting baselines. Across the regimes evaluated, only supervised pretraining on traditional physico-chemical descriptors consistently improves downstream performance for the CLMs tested whereas some forms of pretraining result in models worse than a randomly initialized encoder. While models can resolve molecular structure well, they do so no better than a randomly initialized model, suggesting that, at best, CLMs learn descriptor-like properties in addition to low-level token statistics during pretraining, but surprisingly little chemistry beyond what classical molecular features already capture.

items.title: Autonomous Science Bench: Evaluating AI Agents for Autonomous Scientific Discovery
items.abstract_or_text: AI agents for autonomous scientific discovery must decide which experiments to run under a limited budget. Most benchmarks for science agents provide fixed datasets, while others that support active experimentation largely rely on simulation. We introduce Autonomous Science Bench, an initial release comprising six budgeted design-build-test-learn campaigns grounded in published experiments across biology, chemistry, and materials science. Agents select batches of designs, receive measurements from a lab service, and use the results to guide subsequent experiments before delivering a predictive model. Success requires passing two calibrated gates: a discovery gate, which evaluates the designs the agent measured, and a learning gate, which evaluates its model's ranking of held-out designs. In a pilot evaluation of eight agent-model configurations and 144 trials, the best configuration succeeds in 67% of trials, while the hardest campaign is solved in only three of 24 attempts. The two gates reveal different weaknesses: some agents build accurate rankings but find too few promising designs, while others find promising designs but fail to predict which unseen designs will perform well. These differences are obscured by overall success rates alone. We release version 0.1 of the campaigns, lab runtime, and public leaderboard at https://yibow.me/autonomous-science-bench.

items.title: ATTUNE: Agentic Throughput Tuning for LLM Training
items.abstract_or_text: Training recipes are tuned by hand for one model, cluster and workload, and every new model, accelerator, framework version or dataset means tuning again. Automated tuners search a fixed space of knobs and check only that a job runs, yet a configuration can run to completion while it silently changes training. ATTUNE is a single coding agent that tunes any working recipe for the workload and stack at hand, unattended, within a GPU-hour budget the user sets. It diagnoses each run and changes one lever at a time, guided by a catalog of lessons from past campaigns, and ships a recipe only if it passes a correctness gate: a configuration check against objective-changing settings and known stack defects, and a convergence check of its loss curve against the baseline's. On four held-out models at 64-128 GPUs, ATTUNE raises mean throughput over the strongest public recipe run on our stack by 6.7% on Llama-3.1-405B (best campaign 11.9%) and 33.9% on GLM-4.5 (54.7%), whose public recipe was written for H100. It keeps Mixtral-8x22B's recipe, where nothing it finds clears the noise band. Under a common GPU-hour budget it beats OptiCo, Bayesian optimization and random search on GLM-4.5 and MiniMax-M2; on GLM-4.5 its mean gain is more than four times the best alternative's at less than half the GPU-hours, and on both models its tuning pays for itself within a day of training. The gate rejects no legitimate run and catches 16 of 24 faulty runs, missing only ones that barely move the 20-step loss. Ablations tie its best campaigns to one of its search rules: retrying an out-of-memory layout with recomputation. We release ATTUNE's code and TrainingThroughputBench, a leaderboard of the fastest known recipes for MoE models up to 744B parameters on up to 256 GPUs, each with its throughput, cost per million tokens and a passed correctness check, at https://github.com/amazon-science/attune.

items.title: Microstructural, Energy-Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy, and Fourier-Transform Infrared Analysis of Inorganic-Platelet Polymer Composites for Sustainable Infrastructure
items.abstract_or_text: Polymer matrix composites used in wet or thermally variable environments may change through moisture diffusion, polymer relaxation, swelling and plasticization, hydrolysis or leaching, microcracking, and progressive weakening of the reinforcement–matrix interface. This paper focuses on understanding the composition and morphology of a reinforcing phase, and determining whether its incorporation produces additional bulk-resolvable chemical features, which is important for interpreting composites used in wet or aggressive environments. The study presents a structural and spectroscopic characterization of a commercial glass-flake-reinforced unsaturated-polyester composite by combining energydispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) with full-range Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) against a neat unsaturated-polyester-resin control. EDS gives a composition consistent with a sodium–calcium silicate glass phase for the flake (17.4 wt% Si, 5.0 wt% Na, 2.2 wt% Ca, 1.1 wt% Al, 1.0 wt% Mg and 55.6 wt% O), whereas the polyester matrix and coat regions are dominated by carbon and oxygen (70–75 wt% C and 23–26 wt% O). Two representative flakes (n = 2) have apparent length-to-width ratios of 21.9 and 43.9. FTIR spectra collected over 428–4500 cm-1 show the same principal polyester-resin-associated bands at essentially identical wavenumbers in the composite and neat resin. Polymer-associated band intensities are 12–28% lower in the composite, while the band near the Si–O–Si network bending region changes by only −0.6%. No additional resolvable bulk absorption bands are observed. The results support a physically dispersed silicate-glass phase within the polyester matrix but do not exclude weak or spatially localized interfacial interactions below the resolution of the measurements. The spectra and elemental tables are released as a reusable dataset.

items.title: What Do Foundation Models for Market Microstructure Learn? A Controlled Study with Synthetic Limit Order Books
items.abstract_or_text: Autoregressive transformers trained on limit order book (LOB) message streams are increasingly proposed as foundation models for market microstructure. Because the generative process of real markets is unknown, these models can be judged only by the realism of their output, leaving open what they actually learn. We make the question answerable by inverting the setup: we train GPT-style models on order flow from simulators whose latent parameters are known, so that the Bayes-optimal predictor, the generating state, and the exact data entropy serve as references. Measured against them, next-token pretraining on order flow implements amortized Bayesian inference over market regimes. The learned predictive matches the exact Bayes optimum to within a millinat per token and approaches the oracle floor even on a nonstationary family whose latent state drifts within an episode, a regime that requires filtering. The latent regime is linearly decodable from frozen activations, well above baselines, so a frozen-model read-out calibrates simulator parameters more accurately than windowed maximum likelihood at a fraction of the cost. In our experiments these capabilities are not produced by scale: capacity and token volume saturate early, and it is the diversity of training regimes, not the token count, that determines generalization to unseen markets. On real NASDAQ data, zero-shot transfer is set by how well the simulator prior covers real flow: an enriched mixture nearly closes the gap to an in-domain baseline, and pretraining beats from-scratch training at every budget across held-out tickers. Known ground truth turns average next-token loss, which is uninformative near the entropy floor, into an exact comparison against the Bayes-optimal and oracle predictors.

items.title: Spatial Tumour Tissue Distribution Dynamics of a Bicycle Peptide-MMAE Toxin Conjugate Profiled by Targeted Mass Spectrometry
items.abstract_or_text: A highly specific-NECTIN-4 binding bicyclic peptide covalently linked to the cytotoxin monomethyl auristatin E (MMAE) via a valine-citrulline cleavable linker (zelenectide pevedotin, BT8009) is a promising modality to treat cancer patients with solid tumours. Although the pharmacokinetics and biodistribution of zelenectide pevedotin have been well characterised, a more precise view of tumour delivery and intra-tumoural distribution of its released payload is lacking. To address this, we have developed an approach to profile the spatial tumour and healthy tissue distribution of this anti-cancer agent using laser capture microdissection coupled to targeted liquid chromatography parallel reaction monitoring (LCM-LC-PRM) mass spectrometry. This LCM-assisted spatial pharmacology workflow enables the precise isolation of specific tissue regions, followed by high-resolution analysis of MMAE distribution at sub-tissue-specific levels. By identifying and optimising MS/MS-specific fragmentation ions for accurate and sensitive detection and quantitation of MMAE released from zelenectide pevedotin within tumour tissues, we observed progressive accumulation and sustained retention of MMAE in mouse tumour tissues over a period of 24 h. Conversely, in plasma, liver and muscle tissues, MMAE levels generally declined following early exposure, although inter-animal variability was observed. LCM-based intra-tumour spatial profiling revealed heterogeneous MMAE distribution between tumour cell-rich and stroma-rich regions, with distinct temporal patterns across compartments. Together, our spatial targeted MS method provided valuable insights into zelenectide pevedotin's payload distribution dynamics in vivo, thereby enhancing our understanding of its therapeutic potential and guiding the development of next-generation Bicycle Drug Conjugate (BDC).

items.title: Protein novelty, sequence similarity, and negative sampling controls reveal benchmark specific discrimination in protein protein interactionprediction
items.abstract_or_text: Protein protein interaction (PPI) predictors are often evaluated with random pair splits that permit proteins to recur across training and test sets, while constructed negative pairs can introduce a separate source of benchmark-specific signal. We reassessed the Guo yeast benchmark using a matched protein novelty curve, independently generated MMseqs2 sequence cluster controlled R3 variants, topology only controls, degree- and length matched putative negatives, handcrafted and frozen protein language model representations, multiple model configurations, seed analyses, and connected component aware inference. In the matched R1[->]R2[->]R3 comparison, AAC+CTD-MLP ROC-AUC declined from 0.697 for seen-seen pairs to 0.626 for one-unseen pairs and 0.587 for both-unseen pairs. Across independently regenerated cluster-disjoint R3 variants at 50%, 40%, 30%, and 20% MMseqs2 clustering thresholds, performance showed no consistent monotonic trend. Guo original-negative endpoints had lower positive-network degree than positive endpoints (mean 3.34 versus 6.72), and a degree-only logistic model reached ROC-AUC 0.962 on the original negatives but 0.502 on degree-matched negatives. We used degree-matched negatives consistently for R3 training and testing; six sequence based model configurations yielded ROC-AUC 0.493- 0.547; none showed corrected connected-component-aware evidence of above-chance discrimination. A PIPR multispecies analysis reproduced degree-associated label separation but also exposed cross-species pairing as an additional pooled cue. These results show that protein novelty, operational sequence cluster separation, and negative-set topology are distinct dimensions of PPI benchmark evaluation. The Guo result is benchmark-specific and should not be generalized to sequence-based PPI prediction or protein language models overall. The dataset and source code for the experiments are publicly available at https://github.com/morufwork/guoAudit.git.

items.title: Deep Generative Models for Phylogenetic Inference with Complex Evolutionary Processes
items.abstract_or_text: Inference of phylogenetic trees from sequences plays a central role in understanding evolutionary relationships, with applications ranging from tracking pathogen spread to reconstructing the history of life. Conventionally, practitioners obtain posteriors over trees using likelihood-based methods like MCMC. However, likelihoods are only available for simple evolutionary models with restrictive assumptions. For realistic evolutionary models, inference using conventional methods is prohibitively expensive, inaccurate, or even impossible. In practice, practitioners settle for using as flexible a conventional method as possible, even though they expect it is misspecified. In principle, we could use simulation-based inference: simulate tree and sequence data from an evolutionary model and train a neural network to predict the posterior over trees given sequences. However it is a mathematical challenge to represent and train complex posterior distributions over trees. Here we present a flexible family of conditional generative models over trees. Our models iteratively build trees using three natural paradigms -- top-down, middle-out, or bottom-up -- and are trained using a discrete diffusion framework. For real and synthetic datasets of up to 65 taxa and >10^5 tokens, our models recover MCMC posteriors much more accurately than the previous state-of-the-art simulation-based method Phyloformer 2. Finally, we compare to IQ-Tree, a popular flexible-but-misspecified conventional method. Our models match its tree estimates on simple data, but on more realistic data, our method is reliably more accurate.

items.title: Joint Neural Posterior Estimation and Model Selection for Chemical Reaction Networks
items.abstract_or_text: Simulation-based Bayesian inference for Chemical Reaction Networks (CRNs) must simultaneously solve two computationally demanding problems: discriminating between overlapping reaction pathways and estimating reaction rate constants. Classical approaches, such as Sequential Monte Carlo ABC, rely on handcrafted summary statistics and scale poorly across large parameter spaces. To overcome this, we introduce a neural inference architecture. Our pipeline utilizes shared 1D-CNNs and a permutation-invariant Set Attention mechanism to learn low-dimensional summary statistics from variable-length, multi-experiment time-series data. These statistics simultaneously condition a model selection network to compute posterior model probabilities and model-specific conditional Invertible Neural Networks (cINNs) that estimate parameter posterior distributions. We demonstrate the practical utility of our approach on a real protodeboronation example, illustrating how it handles structural ambiguity and extracts kinetic parameters from competing catalyst deactivation pathways.

items.title: Diff Diffusion: Predicting Edit Paths with Diffusion Models for Efficient Code Editing
items.abstract_or_text: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) are appealing for code generation because they can update many tokens in parallel, yet many are optimized for sequence synthesis rather than edit prediction. This setting is poorly matched to modern AI-assisted IDEs, where edit prediction must infer the next code change from recent edits, the current file, and cursor-local context. Such changes are usually sparse and preserve most source tokens, so regenerating a full code segment wastes computation. We propose Diff Diffusion, a diffusion-inspired LLM framework for code editing that predicts edit paths from an original snippet to its revised form. Diff Diffusion represents denoising as structured edit operations, and combines this formulation with multi-stage training and efficient parallel decoding. By focusing computation on changed regions, Diff Diffusion supports accurate low-latency edits and multi-position parallel modification. Across public edit-completion benchmarks, edit-prediction evaluations, and online validation, Diff Diffusion matches or leads autoregressive baselines while delivering 2.78 times faster inference on public edit-completion benchmarks and a 39.0% P50 model-latency reduction in production. This work provides a new modeling perspective for AI applications that require high accuracy and low latency.

items.title: Coupled Harness--Model Evolution for Scientific Equation Discovery
items.abstract_or_text: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to discover scientific equations from experimental data. Such a discovery system has two parts that must work together: a library of executable computational tools and the model's tool-use policy. The tools supply the solving capability, from diagnosing structure in the data to fitting candidate equations; the policy plans and orchestrates their use. Yet existing systems adapt only one part, keeping either the toolset or the model fixed, which leaves the corresponding failures uncorrectable. We develop a coupled evolution framework that improves both parts from the same verifiable fit-error signal. In the tool-evolution phase, an agent grows an executable tool library from a small set of generic numerical operations by diagnosing its own failures: it authors a new tool when a capability is missing and revises its selection rules when the right tool went unused. In the policy-evolution phase, a small open model (roughly 3B active parameters) is fine-tuned on successful tool-use trajectories collected with the frozen library, on training formulas screened to be disjoint from all evaluation benchmarks. Ablations show the two phases are complementary: with no tool library at all the same model solves almost nothing, the tools account for most of the gain, and trajectory training adds a further gain that is largest on the most difficult problems. The full system solves 79.1/71.3\% of LSR-Synth problems at fit tolerances 10^{-2}/10^{-3}, reaches 63.8\% pooled accuracy on the distributionally different SRSD-Feynman panel, and obtains a normalized CP3-28 aggregate of -7.27. These results suggest a broader recipe for scientific agents: let the model and its instruments improve each other under verifiable feedback.

items.title: OpenDepth: Repurposing Image Editing Priors for Robust Open-World Monocular Depth Estimation
items.abstract_or_text: Recently, the integration of generative priors has revolutionized Monocular Depth Estimation (MDE), achieving state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance with remarkably high data efficiency. However, although methods based on Text-to-Image (T2I) models excel in general scenes, their efficacy degrades sharply when confronted with open-world environmental perturbations, such as illumination variations and adverse weather. Since T2I priors are optimized for semantic synthesis rather than preserving pixel-level structure, they struggle to decouple geometry from appearance under severe visual shifts, easily triggering structural hallucinations. Therefore, our core insight is to model open-world depth estimation as consistent geometric inference across multi-style images, fully leveraging the powerful structure-preserving editing priors of Image-to-Image (I2I) models. Based on this, we propose OpenDepth, a robust open-world MDE framework that introduces "Intra-Domain Awareness" -- the capability to map diverse stylistic inputs sharing identical geometry into a unified latent space. To achieve this, we first align shallow features within the Diffusion Transformer (DiT) to anchor degraded observations to unified geometric representations. Additionally, we introduce a joint RGB latent reconstruction task, requiring the model to recover clean RGB information from degraded inputs. This multi-stage strategy effectively decouples environmental style interference, compelling the model to focus strictly on underlying geometric recovery. Extensive evaluations show that OpenDepth sets new SOTA records for robust zero-shot depth estimation across standard and extreme weather benchmarks, demonstrating exceptional structural integrity and adaptability.

items.title: CPIExtract: A software package to collect and harmonize small molecule and protein interactions
items.abstract_or_text: Summary: The binding interactions between small molecules and proteins are the basis of cellular functions. Yet, experimental data available regarding compound-protein interaction are not harmonized into a single entity but rather scattered across multiple institutions, each maintaining databases with different formats. Extracting information from these multiple sources remains challenging due to data heterogeneity. Here, we present CPIExtract (Compound-Protein Interaction Extract), a tool to interactively extract experimental binding interaction data from multiple databases, perform filtering, and harmonize the resulting information, thus providing a gain of compound-protein interaction data. When compared to a single source, DrugBank, we show that it can collect more than ten times the number of annotations. The end-user can apply custom filtering to the aggregated output data and save it in any generic tabular file suitable for further downstream tasks such as network medicine analyses for drug repurposing and cross-validation of deep learning models. Availability: CPIExtract is an open-source Python package under an MIT license. CPIExtract can be installed from https://pypi.org/project/cpiextract and downloaded from https://github.com/menicgiulia/CPIExtract. The package can run on any standard desktop computer or computing cluster.

items.title: Structural Resolution in Feature Attribution Analysis of Molecular Graph Neural Networks
items.abstract_or_text: Machine learning models based on molecular graphs can evaluate the contribution of each atom to a prediction using feature attribution methods. However, in chemistry, molecular properties are frequently discussed in terms of both individual atoms and structural units comprising multiple atoms, e.g., functional groups and substituents. In this study, we defined the granularity of the structural units used to present and evaluate feature attributions as their structural resolution, and we investigated how the relationship between feature attributions obtained from different molecular graph models varied with structural resolution. These attributions were evaluated at two structural resolutions, i.e., individual atoms and chemically defined structural groups. The group-level feature attributions exhibited higher intermodel agreement than the corresponding atom-level attributions for every target property and model pair. These results indicate that although the allocation of contributions to individual atoms can vary depending on the model architecture, the contribution patterns shared across multiple models can be retained at the level of entire structural groups.

items.title: Synthesis of Amphiphilic Polymer Co-Networks via the Growth of a Living RAFT Network. Part III: Effect of DMSO Content
items.abstract_or_text: Owing to their distinctive nanophase-separated, co-continuous morphology, Amphiphilic polymer co-networks (APCNs) have attracted considerable attention in the past four decades. In 2024, a RAFT-mediated network growth strategy for the synthesis of APCNs was reported. This approach involves first preparing a parent RAFT network, typically a hydrophilic network containing dormant network-RAFT agents, followed by the diffusion and polymerization of hydrophobic monomers within the parent network. This process generates a secondary hydrophobic nanophase within the pre-existing hydrophilic continuous phase, yielding an amphiphilic polymer co-network that fulfils the defining structural characteristics of APCNs. This work reports a systematic study of the effect of DMSO content (10%, 50%, and 75%) on the synthesis of amphiphilic polymer co-networks (APCNs) using the above-mentioned RAFT-mediated network growth strategy. The resulting APCNs comprise a hydrophilic parent network based on oligo(ethylene glycol) methyl ether acrylate (OEGA, Mn = 480) and the crosslinker N, N′-methylenebisacrylamide (Bis), into which hydrophobic n-butyl acrylate (BA) segments are incorporated through RAFT-mediated network growth. Network chemical composition, thermal properties, and morphology were characterized using FT-IR, TGA, DSC, and SEM, while amphiphilicity was assessed through equilibrium swelling measurements in water and toluene. The DMSO content employed during parent network synthesis was found to exert a pronounced effect on the properties of the resulting APCNs. Among the systems investigated, the APCN derived from a parent gel prepared in 75% DMSO and subjected to 5 h of photogrowth exhibited the most balanced amphiphilic character, displaying swelling ratios of 10.30 in water and 18.24 in toluene.

items.title: OrionMoE-v1.0: A Mixture-of-Experts Foundation Model for Tabular In-Context Learning
items.abstract_or_text: Tabular foundation models enable in-context learning by predicting unseen observations from a labeled support table without task-specific parameter updates. Despite recent advances, most existing approaches rely on dense architectures that apply the same transformations across features and datasets. We introduce OrionMoE-Small, a compact tabular foundation model that combines distribution-aware representations with dataset-conditioned sparse mixture-of-experts computation. Built on a dual-axis Transformer architecture, OrionMoE-Small selectively activates experts along the feature axis, with routing decisions informed by both individual feature representations and the broader dataset context. This design enables adaptive allocation of computation across heterogeneous tabular problems while retaining a shared computational pathway across tasks. OrionMoE-Small is pretrained entirely on synthetic classification tasks generated from a structured causal prior and performs downstream prediction without gradient-based adaptation. Experiments across multiple tabular benchmarks demonstrate competitive performance against substantially larger foundation models, with particularly strong results on small-context and high-dimensional datasets. Further analysis reveals favorable relative performance under class imbalance and highlights the importance of feature composition.

items.title: HEM-Med: A Hierarchical Agentic Memory Framework for Safe Multi-Center Medication Recommendation
items.abstract_or_text: Medication recommendation (MR) is critical for clinical decision support. While existing MR methods are mostly designed for single-center learning, where only one independent hospital is involved, multi-center MR with hospitals of different scales has become increasingly demanding in practice. In multi center settings, abundant data from large medical centers can improve recommendation performance for low-resource centers. Despite a few preliminary attempts on this task, two critical gaps remain. Gap 1: Existing multi-center methods fail to disentangle transferable cross-hospital clinical experience from hospital-specific prescribing patterns, limiting clinical feasibility and physician acceptance. Gap 2: They commonly overlook multi label safety constraints of MR, including drug-drug interaction risks and local formulary feasibility, which are essential for safe real-world deployment. To address these gaps, we propose HEM-Med, a novel hierarchical agentic memory framework for multi-center MR. To address Gap 1, we design a disentangled hierarchical memory module that builds patient-level medication context attribution records and disentangles them into cross hospital experience memory and hospital-specific residual memory. To address Gap 2, we introduce a safety-aware medication set generation module, which integrates dual-level experience retrieval with safety-aware set decoding to produce clinically relevant, safer, and locally adaptive medication recommendations. Experiments on a real-world multi-center eICU dataset show that HEM-Med outperforms representative transfer learning, LLM-based, and MR baselines in terms of both recommendation accuracy and safety.

items.title: Alkyl-BODIPYs as a Self-Photoredox Catalyst for their Oxidative Hydroxymethylation
items.abstract_or_text: The adoption of photocatalytic approaches for utilising small organic molecules in self‑catalysed reactions offers opportunities in green organic synthesis. We report that alkylated boron‑dipyrromethenes (BODIPYs) act as self‑photoredox catalysts for their own oxidation under mild visible‑light conditions. Using an imidazolinium salt (NHC-H) as a quencher, alkylated BODIPYs are oxidised cleanly to the corresponding hydroxymethyl derivatives in a one‑pot process. Luminescence studies, including Stern–Volmer analysis, support a reductive‑quenching pathway in which the NHC-H transfers an electron to photoexcited BODIPY to give a BODIPY radical anion. The method proceeds without external photocatalysts or stoichiometric oxidants and shows good functional‑group tolerance, highlighting the potential of these chromophores both as substrates and catalytic light absorbers. Moreover, the synthesized molecules were demonstrated to behave as effective passivating agents for layered Mn2+

items.title: SolBehave: Evaluating the Behavioural Correctness of LLM-Generated Smart Contracts
items.abstract_or_text: Large language models increasingly generate Solidity smart contracts that, once deployed, can never be patched, making a single latent fault permanent and exploitable. Yet current evaluations mostly ask only whether generated code compiles. We introduce SolBehave, a benchmark for evaluating the correctness of model-generated contracts at scale, moving beyond ad hoc unit tests. Across 250 real, reproducible Ethereum contracts, we apply three complementary tests of behavioural fidelity: differential fuzzing, historical-transaction replay, and, as our core contribution, synthetic-transaction replay guided by a Dynamic Condition Response (DCR) graph that enumerates the space of legitimate function-call sequences. Differential fuzzing compares each generated function with the original on automatically generated inputs; historical replay compares the whole contract on the transactions it actually received on-chain; DCR-guided replay compares it on sequences of calls that follow its intended usage, including orderings that never occurred on-chain. We evaluate seven state-of-the-art open-weight models after one round of automated repair. Compilation success ranges from 26.4% to 92.7%, but under differential fuzzing only 31.4% of all generated function bodies that compile, pooled over models and samples, are equivalent to the original. Divergence at the contract level is the norm rather than the exception: for six of the seven models, between 13% and 31% of the generated contracts that compile diverge from the original under historical replay, and between 13% and 44% under DCR-guided replay; only Gemma-4-31B stays below 3% on both. Compilation is therefore a necessary condition for correctness and far from a sufficient one.

items.title: Agaram 2.5B: The First Tamil-First Language Model Trained from Scratch with Tool Calling. A Playbook for Under-Represented Languages
items.abstract_or_text: We trained Agaram 2.5B, a 2.5-billion-parameter Tamil-English language model, from scratch on about 50 billion tokens (58% Tamil, the rest English, math, code and parallel text) on one node of eight H100 GPUs in about six days, with a new tokenizer that, unlike our first model's, keeps line breaks. Supervised fine-tuning on 134,428 conversations, whose replies an open-weight teacher model wrote, and three short targeted rounds turned it into a chat model that answers in Tamil script, romanized Tamil (Tanglish) and English and can call tools: on 25 tool prompts whose schemas appear in training it picks the right tool 23 times and gives exactly the expected arguments 13 times. The released model translates better than Sarvam-1, a 2B Indic base model, in all six FLORES and IN22 directions (FLORES chrF 54.3 into Tamil and 55.2 into English, against 49.2 and 44.2), and nearly doubles its base model on native-Tamil IndicIFEval (19.3% from 10.0%). It is weak on knowledge: reading-comprehension and knowledge benchmarks sit near chance, and on 50 held-out everyday questions written by one native speaker, one LLM judge rated 46% of its replies usable (22-24 of 50 over three passes; 95% interval for 23 of 50, 33-60%), with nearly every failure a wrong fact. Our two further SFT experiments changed answer format but not the knowledge measures. We also describe our first model, Agaram 1.5B, whose failures shaped the choices here; how the judge's scores varied between passes on identical replies; and, item by item, what the targeted rounds trained against and where frontier-model text entered the data. The project ran on compute credits and our own funds, about USD 13,300 across both models; the weights are released (licence to be announced after legal review), with GGUF files for llama.cpp, at https://huggingface.co/murai-labs/agaram-2.5b-instruct; code at https://github.com/Murai-Labs/Agaram2.5b

items.title: LifeSearch: Benchmarking Deep Research Agents for Real-World Life and Productivity
items.abstract_or_text: Deep research (DR) agents address open-ended information needs through multi-step reasoning, long-horizon web search, and evidence synthesis. However, existing benchmarks primarily focus on academic research or synthetic tasks, leaving DR agents' capabilities in real-world life and professional productivity settings insufficiently evaluated. To bridge this gap, we introduce LifeSearch, a challenging benchmark comprising 203 Chinese and English tasks derived from real-user query seeds across 7 concrete life and productivity domains. With more than 4,500 hours of human annotation, we construct over 4,000 expert-written, fine-grained rubrics, covering both report-content criteria for coverage and accuracy and concrete criteria specifying values, units, dates, and URLs. We conduct extensive experiments on 12 advanced DR agents under a unified evaluation harness, systematically analyzing their performance patterns and failure modes. We find that even the best-performing frontier agent, GPT-5.6 Sol, achieves a score of only 63.4%, leaving substantial room for improvement on realistic life and professional DR tasks. We select the grading configuration by comparing candidate LLM judges against human rubric labels, and a human ranking study shows strong alignment between aggregate benchmark scores and human judgments (Spearman's ρ= 0.89, Kendall's τ= 0.81). LifeSearch provides a rigorous evaluation framework and foundation for advancing DR agents toward real-world life and productivity.

items.title: Can Machine Learning Potentials Be More Accurate Than the Methods They Are Trained On?
items.abstract_or_text: Although machine learning potentials (MLPs) generalize across configurational and chemical compound spaces, their accuracy is commonly believed to be limited by their training methods, with improvements beyond this limit achieved so far only by refitting to experimental observables. In this Perspective, we argue that MLPs can also be made more accurate than their training methods non-empirically by generalizing across a third space, that of quantum-chemical methods. We propose routes to method-transferable MLPs that predict at unseen methods, with working implementations in both density-functional and wavefunction-based theories showing that they can be more accurate than any of their training methods. Aiming beyond the accuracy of the training methods could also make universal MLPs more accurate than single-method models, even when the method-transferable MLPs remain less accurate than those QM methods. Method-transferable MLPs will shape the construction of training datasets and the evaluation of models, pushing the accuracy limits of chemical simulations.

items.title: QK-Edit: Revisiting Attention-based Injection in MM-DiT for Image and Video Editing
items.abstract_or_text: Multimodal Diffusion Transformers (MM-DiTs) have recently emerged as a powerful framework for unified text-vision synthesis, surpassing traditional U-Net architectures in generative tasks. One key innovation lies in its Multimodal Self-Attention (MM-SA) interaction, where image and text tokens are concatenated and processed via self-attention. However, this mechanism poses significant challenges for editing, rendering conventional U-Net-based attention manipulation methods ineffective. To address this limitation, we propose QK-Edit, a training-free framework that exploits the unique attention dynamics of MM-DiTs for precise text-guided image and video editing. By introducing a novel query-key manipulation strategy, our method isolates and adjusts critical attention components to achieve an optimal balance between prompt fidelity and structural consistency. This enables seamless edits across various tasks, including object addition, object removal, object replacement, changing background, changing material, changing color, and style transformation. Notably, it can be easily implemented with feature replacement in inference. QK-Edit demonstrates superior editing performance on state-of-the-art models, such as FLUX and HunyuanVideo, effectively bridging the gap between generative power and editable flexibility in MM-DiTs, and paving the way for scalable multimodal content creation.

items.title: Stable triorganoiodine complexes
items.abstract_or_text: The first examples of air stable acyclic triorganoiodine compounds, phenyliodine bis(1-(2-R)-o-carborane)s have been isolated from reactions of PhIL2 reagents with lithio-o-carboranes and crystallographically characterized. When R = H or Si(CH3)3, the complexes are predisposed to form o-carboryne through β-elimination as confirmed by a trapping reaction with naphthalene, where the R = H variant degrades during formation. The latter Si(CH3)3 derivative is isolable in modest yield, while for R = CH3, the resulting phenyliodine bis(1-(2-methyl)-o-carborane)s can be obtained in high yields. The complexes known so far appear to behave as nonnucleophilic bases, and treatment with strong protic acids affords more electrophilic phenyl(1-o-carboranyl) iodonium salts. Compared with our previous synthesis of an aryl(1-o-carboranyl) iodonium salt, this method is simpler and offers broadened scope. Less is known of these salts than previously assumed as earlier reports have now also been found incorrect. A preliminary study finds they can either arylate or 1-o-carboranylate a chloride nucleophile with chemoselectivity tuneable by electronic modification of the oCb ligand, providing a rare example of an o-carborane C atom reacting as an electrophile.

items.title: PrismaCoder: Pushing the Boundaries of Open Multimodal Code Intelligence through Decomposed Rubric Synthesis
items.abstract_or_text: Multimodal code intelligence connects the symbolic world of programs with the visual world their execution creates. Interest in this capability is burgeoning, as models are increasingly asked to produce charts, webpages, animations, and semi-structured documents. Recently, proprietary models have pushed far ahead, producing interactive artifacts even from a text description or a screenshot alone. Yet their data and training remain closed, and open progress is held back by the quantity and quality of available data and by the pipelines and methods for producing it. Quality is the harder of the two, since a sample must be correct as a program, well built, and above all visually right once rendered. No existing signal covers all three. Execution often returns just a pass or fail, code similarity does not map to the visual output, and task-specific verifiers do not generalize. To push open progress further, we start from the data side with PrismaForge, a hierarchical data pipeline centered on a synthesized rubric that decomposes these factors into checkable criteria. The same rubric serves as both filter and reward: it curates the supervised corpus, then drives reinforcement learning on visual-coding tasks. Leveraging PrismaForge for data synthesis and filtering, we build PrismaCoder-2M, the most diverse open dataset for multimodal code intelligence and the largest to date. On the model side, we train PrismaCoder-9B and PrismaCoder-35B on this data and release both. They lead the open state of the art by a wide margin and rival leading proprietary systems. Our analyses further show that the proposed rubric-based pipeline improves multimodal coding performance across model backbones. We release our code and data at https://qiushisun.github.io/PrismaCoder-Home/.

items.title: Interlock: From Local Correctness to Task Completion in Long-Horizon Agents
items.abstract_or_text: Large language model agents increasingly undertake long-horizon tasks in complex environments characterized by fragmented evidence, partially completed states, and dependencies across resources and artifacts. Existing agents may satisfy individual requirements while failing to maintain these relationships, producing locally correct but incomplete outcomes. These failures arise because task completion depends on relationships among environmental evidence, consequential decisions, and required effects. To address this completion gap, we propose Interlock, a framework for task synthesis that represents each task as a typed completion graph. Grounding edges connect public evidence to decisions, coupling hyperedges impose joint constraints across components, and realization edges connect decisions to all required downstream effects. Interlock compiles this graph into a resettable workspace, a public request, and an evaluation rubric. A source-coverage review checks whether the original requirements survive generation, while a public-input review checks whether the rubric is supported by the materials available to the solver. An agent-as-judge inspects execution artifacts and runs verification scripts, retaining trajectories judged to satisfy all mandatory requirements.
